analysis.one_liner: Bans forced arbitration clauses in employment, consumer, antitrust, and civil rights disputes.
analysis.headline: Despite 39 Senate cosponsors, the bill received no committee vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Most American workers and consumers sign contracts — job applications, credit card agreements, app terms of service — that require any future dispute to be decided by a private arbitrator chosen under company rules, and that bar them from joining class actions. This bill would make such pre-dispute clauses unenforceable for employment, consumer, antitrust, and civil rights disputes, restoring the right to go to court and to sue as a group. It also covers independent contractors and leaves union grievance-arbitration procedures untouched.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers, consumers, and small businesses who have signed arbitration clauses: they could take discrimination, wage, fraud, and other claims to court instead of private arbitration, and could join class or collective actions again.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and consumers with arbitration clauses

how_it_helps.text: No pre-dispute arbitration agreement or pre-dispute class-action waiver would be valid or enforceable for employment, consumer, antitrust, or civil rights disputes, so individuals could take those disputes to court.
Employment disputes are covered regardless of whether the worker is classified as an employee or an independent contractor, closing a common misclassification loophole.
A court, not an arbitrator, decides whether the law applies, even if the contract tries to delegate that question to the arbitrator.
Arbitration provisions in union collective bargaining agreements are preserved, except they cannot waive a worker's right to judicial enforcement of constitutional or statutory rights.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that use arbitration clauses to resolve disputes privately and avoid class actions — employers across industries, banks, credit card issuers, telecoms, and tech platforms — would face more court cases and class actions, higher litigation costs, and greater exposure to damages.

drawbacks.text: Arbitration can be faster and cheaper than court for an individual claim, so some single plaintiffs might prefer it; the bill keeps voluntary post-dispute arbitration available but removes it as a condition of the original deal.
Restoring class actions raises litigation costs and settlement exposure for companies, costs that businesses may pass along in prices or that small firms may find hardest to absorb.
The bill applies retroactively only to future disputes, so people whose claims were already filed under existing clauses get no relief.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the tens of millions of workers and consumers bound by arbitration clauses, the bill restores a meaningful remedy: private arbitration tends to produce smaller, unappealable awards decided under rules the company helped choose, and class-action bans make small-value fraud and wage claims uneconomical to bring alone. The cost falls on businesses in higher litigation exposure, which is precisely the exposure the current system shields them from. The main honest trade-off is speed and cost in individual cases, which the bill partially addresses by leaving voluntary arbitration intact.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred the bill to the Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up; it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Blumenthal introduced the Forced Arbitration Injustice Repeal Act on March 1, 2021, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee that same day.
The bill attracted 39 cosponsors — 38 of the Senate's 48 Democrats and 1 of its 2 independents — but no Republicans.
The Judiciary Committee held no markup or vote on the bill during the two-year Congress, and it never reached the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that rely on forced arbitration clauses to keep disputes out of court and out of class actions kept that shield, because the bill died in committee without a vote.

for.name: Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on March 1, 2021.

for.name: 38 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 Senate independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it the support of nearly every Senate Democrat but none of the chamber's 50 Republicans.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Dick Durbin (D)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill in two years, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and business groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislation to invalidate mandatory arbitration clauses, arguing arbitration is faster and cheaper and warning of class-action litigation costs.

sides.party_line_note: All 39 cosponsors were Democrats or independents; no Republican signed on, and with no committee or floor action ever scheduled, the bill's fate was decided by inaction rather than a recorded vote.

industries.note: Employers widely use pre-dispute arbitration clauses and class-action waivers in hiring paperwork; the bill would expose them to court suits and collective wage-and-hour actions. Their cost is workers' regained access to court and class remedies.

industries.industry: Banks, credit card issuers, and consumer finance firms
industries.note: Consumer credit agreements routinely force cardholders and borrowers into arbitration; the bill would let consumers sue and band together in class actions over fees, fraud, and credit disputes.
Terms-of-service arbitration clauses, including for digital services, would become unenforceable, opening platforms to consumer and civil rights suits.
Lawyers who bring employment, consumer, and civil rights class actions would regain the case volume that class-action waivers have eliminated; their gain is the public's regained access to a remedy.
